messages.text: Why do they divide the dot products by √dₖ?

Each score is a dot product, $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$. If the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, that sum has mean 0 and variance $d_k$, so its typical size grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$ [S1].

With $d_k = 64$, the scores for one query end up far apart, and softmax puts almost all of the weight on the largest. In that flat region its gradients are tiny, so the model learns slowly [S1].

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ brings the variance back to 1, which keeps softmax where small changes in the scores still matter:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

The paper motivates this with a comparison: additive attention beats unscaled dot-product attention once $d_k$ is large, and the scaling closes that gap [S1]. The rest of the mechanism, mapping a query and key–value pairs to a weighted sum of the values, is unchanged [S2].

gaps.name: Scaled dot-product attention
gaps.description: Attention that weights values by the softmax of query-key dot products, each divided by the square root of the key dimension to keep scores moderate.

gaps.name: Variance
gaps.description: The expected squared distance of a random variable from its mean, measuring how spread out its values are.

quote.text: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

messages.text:
One attention head produces a single weighted average of the values for each position. If a word needs to pull in two different things at once, say its subject and the adjective describing it, that one average blurs them together. That is what “averaging inhibits this” refers to [S1].

Multi-head attention runs $h = 8$ smaller attention functions side by side. Each head has its own learned projections of the queries, keys and values, so each can look for a different kind of relationship. Their outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model width [S1].

- Each head works in $d_k = d_v = 64$ dimensions instead of 512, so the total cost stays close to one full-width head [S1].
- Inside every head the computation is the same scaled dot-product attention as before [S2].
